result.summary: Pindar celebrates Timasarchos of Aigina, a young wrestling victor at Nemea, praising song as the best cure for toil. He recalls the victories of Timasarchos and his late father, the heroes of the Aiakid line (Telamon, Peleus, Teukros, Achilles), and the praise due to his uncle Kallikles.

scenes.title: Editor's note on the ode
scenes.summary: The editor says the date is unknown and the ode was probably sung in a procession on the winner's return.

scenes.title: Song as healer; victories listed
scenes.summary: Pindar says praise-song soothes toil better than warm water, dedicates the hymn to Zeus, Nemea and Timasarchos, and lists the victories won at Kleonai, Athens and Thebes.

scenes.title: Telamon and Herakles at Troy
scenes.summary: Pindar briefly tells how Telamon helped Herakles destroy Troy and slay Alkyoneus, then breaks off for lack of time.
scenes.stakes: Telamon and Herakles face a terrible giant and his hordes.

scenes.title: Encouragement and the lute
scenes.summary: Pindar urges bearing up against enemies and bids his lute weave a strain for Oinone and Cyprus.
scenes.stakes: Envious enemies threaten the poet and his patrons.

scenes.title: Aiakid heroes and Peleus
scenes.summary: Pindar lists the realms of Aiakos' descendants and tells how Peleus escaped Akastos' wife's plot and married a Nereid, then turns his ship back from Gadeira.
scenes.stakes: Peleus is threatened with death by ambush, fire, lion and teeth.

scenes.title: Praise for the clan and Kallikles
scenes.summary: Pindar praises the clan's games victories and offers a song for Kallikles, the uncle, and Euphanes, the grandsire, ending on Melesias, the trainer.

alias_notes.explanation: Patronymic used for Akastos in the plot against Peleus.
Descendants of Aiakos, the Aiginetan heroic line.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable claim that speech outlives deeds when drawn from the heart.
Song refines a man's deeds like gold, making him a peer of kings.
Famous marker of the world's western limit at Gadeira.

analysis.text: Poetry is presented as healing and as the means by which achievement is preserved beyond the deed itself.
The ode honors an Aiginetan athlete by linking him to the island's mythic Aiakid heroes, reflecting how victory songs tied families and cities to heroic ancestry.

fun_facts.text: Pindar's mention that none may pass beyond Gadeira (modern Cádiz) reflects the Greek view of the Straits of Gibraltar as the edge of the world.

language_notes.text: The war between Athens and Aigina broke out later; Pindar's friendly mention of Athens suggests the ode predates it.
"Hath" and "festive joy" are archaic or formal; the line says celebration and song are the best remedy after labour, meaning the athlete's training and contest.
The Aiakids were the descendants of Aiakos, legendary kings of Aigina; their stronghold means the island's city. Timasarchos is from Aigina.
"Erewhile" means "a while ago"; "nothing loth" means willingly. "A chain of wreaths" means a series of victories.
Amphitryon was Herakles' mortal stepfather and buried at Thebes, where the games honoured him; his tomb lay beside the contest site.
Telamon, king of Aigina and father of Ajax, sacked Troy with Herakles; Alkyoneus was a giant, and the Meropes were people of Kos whom Herakles fought.
The feast of the new moon was a monthly celebration; Pindar says he is drawn on to the celebration of the victory, leaving the long myth.
"Weave this woof" treats composing a song as weaving; "Lydian harmony" names a musical mode, here described as sweet and suited to praise.
Peleus sacked Iolkos after Akastos' wife Hippolyte falsely accused him when he refused her. The Haimones are the Thessalians, to whom Iolkos was made subject.
Peleus' sword was hidden by Akastos; the centaur Cheiron recovered it. The fire, lion and teeth refer to the shape-changes of Thetis, whom Peleus held to win her.
Gadeira is modern Cádiz, beyond the Pillars of Heracles; the edge of the known world, so a limit for the poet's praise.
Theandrid: the clan of Timasarchos, descended from Theandros. Isthmos and Nemea are two of the four great Greek games sites.
A pillar whiter than Parian stone means a statue or monument; Paros was famous for its white marble. The song is offered as a finer monument.
The wielder of the trident is Poseidon, god of the Isthmian games; parsley of Corinth refers to the victor's wreath there.

context_notes.text: Odes like this were commissioned to celebrate athletic victors, and could be performed by a chorus when the victor came home.
Nemea in the Peloponnese hosted the Nemean Games in honour of Zeus, where Timasarchos won as a wrestler.
Herakles' earlier sack of Troy, under King Laomedon, came a generation before the Trojan War of Homer.
These are the realms of Aiakos' descendants: Aias at Salamis, Achilles on the White Island, Thetis at Phthia, and Neoptolemos in Epeiros.
Melesias was an Athenian trainer of athletes, here honoured as the one who trained Timasarchos.

literary_notes.text: Joyful celebration and song are called physicians, treating the exhaustion of effort as an illness.
Words of praise are "married" to the lyre's music, presenting poetry and song as a union.
Pindar compresses a boast about poetry's power into a maxim: words outlast deeds.
Pindar abruptly breaks off the myth, claiming lack of time, a typical way to move on from the digression.
Being held by the sea to the waist stands for danger and plots; sailing home in daylight stands for eventual triumph over enemies.
Song is compared to refining gold, which reveals its splendour; praise likewise brings out a man's worth.
The praise-singer is figured as a wrestler grappling with words, which pictures poetry as athletic contest, fitting the ode's subject.
